concept.name: Put debit spread
concept.definition: A put debit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long put at a higher strike and a short put at a lower strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net debit. It is synonymous with the bear put spread: a moderately bearish position with maximum gain and maximum loss both fixed at entry.
concept.intuition: You buy downside participation but sell away the extreme-crash part below the lower strike to make the bearish bet cheaper.
concept.mechanics: Net debit = premium paid minus premium received. Above the higher strike both puts expire worthless and the debit is lost; at or below the lower strike the spread is worth the strike width. It is the put-side counterpart of the bull call spread at equivalent strikes.
concept.formula: Max loss = net debit; max gain = (K2 - K1) - net debit; breakeven = K2 - net debit, where K1 < K2 are the put strikes.
concept.failure_modes: Downside skew often makes the long higher-strike put expensive relative to the short leg, raising the breakeven; the capped payoff misses the bulk of true crash payoffs that outright puts capture.
concept.misconceptions: A put debit spread is not equivalent to shorting stock with limited risk — it decays with time and needs the decline to occur before expiration to reach full value.
concept.example: Buy the XYZ $100 put for $4.00, sell the $95 put for $1.50: net debit $2.50. At or below $95 the spread is worth $5 (gain $250); at or above $100 the $250 debit is lost.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
